Absentee Shawnee

Also find this entry through: Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

Absentee Shawnee histories connect Eastern Woodlands homelands, repeated displacement, and continuing community life in Oklahoma. Tribal publications, constitutional records, language resources and artworks provide different paths into the Big Jim and White Turkey communities and their shared government.

Names & relationshipsAbsentee Shawnee, Eastern Shawnee and the Shawnee Tribe are distinct governments. Shared ancestry and language, and collaboration among their citizens, do not make their programs or political histories interchangeable.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

A distinct Shawnee government and community histories

Three federally recognized Shawnee governments now exist in Oklahoma: the Absentee Shawnee Tribe, Eastern Shawnee Tribe and Shawnee Tribe. The Absentee Shawnee Tribe’s account connects its people with Eastern Woodlands homelands and describes movement into Missouri and Arkansas under colonial pressure, with some communities moving onward into Indian Territory and Texas. It traces the Big Jim community to Little Axe and the White Turkey community to the Shawnee area. The constitution’s preamble names both bands. These are communities within one government; shared Shawnee ancestry and language also connect people across the three governments without making their institutions interchangeable.

Read the sources [1] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma [5] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

02

Dispersal and the meaning of “Absentee”

Article 2 of the 1854 treaty provides especially revealing context for the Absentee distinction. It refers to Shawnee who had been separated from the treaty community and sets conditions for receiving surplus Kansas land if they returned. It distinguishes a five-year return period from a further period involving remaining land or monetary payment. The word “Absentee” thus reflects relationships to Shawnee lands and treaty arrangements in Kansas, rather than an absence of a community or government. Reading the provisions alongside community history shows how federal arrangements tried to redirect dispersed Shawnee people toward Kansas.

Read the sources [2] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

03

Allotment, cession, and landholding in Oklahoma

The June 26, 1890 agreement is a direct source for a later transformation of Absentee Shawnee landholding. Article 1 uses sweeping language relinquishing claims in the described tract to the United States. Article 2 confirms existing allotments, orders completion of others, excludes certain school and federal lands, and authorizes an agent to allot land for people who failed or refused to select it before the specified deadline. Article 3 ties an allowance of 650 allottees to financial deductions for additional allotments; Article 4 promises $65,000 for homes and improvements. White Turkey and five other named leaders signed the instrument. Its legal text records an imposed policy framework, while leaving essential questions about negotiation, dissent and family experiences for further community-centered research.

Read the sources [3] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

04

Constitutions and the distribution of governmental authority

A constitution ratified in December 1938 organized a council of adult members and a business committee under the Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act. It is a historical document, useful for tracing institutional change. The constitution ratified in June 1977, published by the Tribe with later amendments, describes a judicial branch and a legislative/executive branch, together with an independent election body. The General Council consists of members aged eighteen and older. The five elected Executive Committee offices are Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary, Treasurer and Representative; the published 2019 amendment provides four-year terms. Reading the two documents together shows constitutional development rather than a government frozen at its 1938 structure.

Read the sources [4] Absentee-Shawnee Tribe / U.S. Office of Indian Affairs; GovInfo [5] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

05

Language renewal as a governmental priority

The January 2026 tribal newspaper reports creation of a standalone Language/Culture Department, giving language work its own institutional home after earlier placement within Cultural Preservation and the 477 programs. The article recalls the Executive Committee’s December 2022 language emergency and adoption of the Pi Pa Pe Po alphabet. It describes online lessons, QR codes, after-school teaching and plans for further classes with Administration for Native Americans support. Director Scott Miller emphasizes the difference between recognizing words and carrying on a conversation, and the role of children in bringing language into family life. These are dated accounts of priorities and initiatives; they do not establish a current speaker count or prove that every planned class occurred.

Read the sources [6] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

06

Words in daily life and learning across Shawnee communities

The Tribe’s public lexicon organizes vocabulary around everyday activities: greeting someone, eating, household objects, foods, weather and the seasons. English meanings and phonetic aids make it a practical starting point for learners. A separate May 2024 Shawnee Tribe publication introduces its master-apprentice program through participants’ own accounts. Absentee Shawnee elder George “Fife” Blanchard recalls growing up with Shawnee as his first language and describes his commitment to teaching. Absentee Shawnee apprentice Daniel Citty connects learning with his children and relationships among Shawnee communities. Their accounts show how language work can connect people across governments while retaining each participant’s particular identity and experience.

Read the sources [7] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma [8] Shawnee Tribe

07

Protecting ancestors and shaping public history

The April 2024 Cultural Preservation report describes responsibilities extending beyond present Oklahoma settlements. Tribal Historic Preservation Office staff reviewed federal projects and participated in consultation concerning ancestral places, ancestors and funerary belongings. The report also describes work with Ohio History Connection and Ohio’s natural-resources department on interpretation for Great Council State Park. Tribal staff reviewed display wording and advocated use of Pi Pa Pe Po orthography. Library development and Shawnee-centered resources appear in the same report. These activities show cultural preservation as consultation, education and community service. The account records work underway at that date; a consultation should not be described as a completed repatriation.

Read the sources [9] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

08

Ernest Spybuck and the histories carried by paintings

Ernest Spybuck, also recorded as Earnest L. Spybuck, depicted community life in early twentieth-century Oklahoma. Marshall Gettys’s biography emphasizes his work as a farmer as well as a painter, and his relationship with anthropologist M. R. Harrington. Spybuck’s compositions use foreground, background and perspective to show detailed gatherings and activities. The National Museum of the American Indian’s record for Procession Before War Dance identifies him as Absentee Shawnee, dates the work to about 1908, and records Harrington’s purchase from the artist in 1910. Bringing biography and object history together helps readers ask who made an image, how it entered a collection and whose interpretation accompanies it.

Read the sources [10] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [11] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

09

Self-government in health, research, and economic life

The self-governance compact signed with the Indian Health Service in July 2017 describes tribal authority to redesign health programs and allocate resources according to community priorities, alongside continuing federal responsibilities. Its attached funding agreement documents a particular historical funding period. The Health System’s RENEW center offers a contemporary example of institution building: its public account connects pain and behavioral-health research with community advice, tribal approval and ownership of data, while describing a registry and research review board still in development. Economic institution building has its own documentary history. The archived Tribal Development Act identifies employment, revenue, enterprise development and land acquisition as governmental purposes. These sources explain authorities and aspirations; assessing their effects requires separate, dated evidence from community experience and outcomes.

Read the sources [12] Absentee Shawnee Tribe / Indian Health Service [13] Absentee Shawnee Tribal Health System [14] Absentee Shawnee Tribe; archived by University of Oklahoma Law Center

What needs further research

  • Develop more community-authored family and local histories, especially experiences of the Big Jim and White Turkey communities beyond institutional summaries.
  • Reconstruct landholding under the 1872 legislation and 1890–1891 allotment process through tribal interpretation and primary records; do not equate rights to individual allotments with a blanket claim of communal title.
  • Add an Absentee Shawnee account of twentieth-century displacement around Little Axe and Lake Thunderbird, with carefully evaluated records of land acquisition and community rebuilding.
  • Follow up the January 2026 language initiatives with dated community reports on classes, participation and learning; no current fluent-speaker total is asserted.
  • Expand community perspectives on education, livelihoods, arts and stewardship, and check cultural suitability and permissions before reproducing artworks, recordings or ceremonial material.
  • Confirm the latest consolidated constitutional and code amendments with the Tribe when using these materials for a precise legal question; archived enactments and funding agreements have different dates and purposes.
